course_title: Politics, Philosophy, Economics 4: Toward Social and Economic Reform
course_description: PPES4100 Politics, Philosophy, Economics 4: Toward Social and Economic Reform applies a real-life, employability-focused lens that will enable you to draw on and apply the practical and professional skills you have gained during your PPE journey. With a particular emphasis on equality and inequality - a core, substantive area of dispute in resolving complex policy problems - you will engage in a collaborative strategic thinking exercise to address an area of critical uncertainty. This inquiry requires you to think deeply about the life experiences of those affected by inequality to provide thoughtful and creative solutions. You will need to be self-regulating in your research and project development as you integrate knowledge and skills from the three disciplines to create an evidence-based solution to a national concern.

Additional timetable information
This is a 6 unit Honours level course which equates to 30 hours per week of work, 3 hours of which will be spent in seminars or workshops. Students are expected to self-organise their own and group work outside of contact hours to produce work to an honours standard.
course_aims: This course will enable students to integrate their knowledge and skills acquired throughout the PPE program to investigate and address a significant source of social and economic inequality in the Australian context. Working collaboratively and individually, students will propose an evidence-based solution to a chosen problem of inequality, the strategic aim of which is to achieve more equitable outcomes for marginalised groups. Students will be expected to lead an independent inquiry, be self-regulating in their research and project development; and demonstrate a capacity for applying a multidisciplinary approach to problem-solving.

learning_outcomes.description: Integrate knowledge and skills from the three disciplines to work individually and collaboratively to investigate factors underlying inequalities in relation to a chosen problem. A1; A4
Develop effective methods and strategies for communicating with different audiences, including academic, professional, and community groups. B2; B5; B6
Generate an evidence-based solution to a chosen problem of inequality, drawing on research skills commensurate with Honours level. C4
Justify a preferred solution to the problem of inequality being investigated. C5; D3
Adopt a theoretically informed, evidence-based approach to analysing, explaining, and evaluating alternative solutions. D4; D5; D6

Demonstrate insights into different ethical perspectives on the moral issues associated with inequalities for the purpose of grounding the preferred solution on solid moral principles and reasoning. E1; E5

assessment_details.task_description: Due date (presentation for feedback): 6/10/2026 11am. Due date (final submission for scenario plan and group strategy): 9/10/2026, 2pm. Scenario planning task: Policy-making in Australia has historically suffered from 'short-terminism'--strategic thinking and planning bounded within 3 to 4 year election cycles. For wicked problems like entrenched social and economic inequalities, longer-term strategic thinking is required. Imagine you are working for a government office that seeks to break the cycle of short-termism by engaging its staff in more futures thinking. Your target is 2045. What could we as a nation plausibly achieve between now and then that might help to address the problems associated with your specific social and economic inequality? In teams of 4, you are required to engage in a scenario planning strategic thinking exercise, where you are asked to: Identify the driving forces that shape the environment in which your inequality is manifested Identify 2 critical uncertainties and construct a 2x2 matrix Populate the quadrants with plausible scenarios (individual students take responsibility for 1 quadrant each) Generate a group strategy to lead Australia to a preferred future among the possible/ plausible ones identified. This is a five-part task combining individual and group assessment tasks. Part A: Preparation and Planning (Group; hurdle requirement) Students will form themselves or be assigned into groups of four in week 1. The first task is to settle on which inequality your team specifically wants to work on. (Examples include income, wealth, health, educational, housing, racial, ethnic, gender, geographical, age, disability, etc.) Design a Team Charter and a Peer and Self Evaluation form to to ensure equal contributions, effective communication, and respectful disagreement resolution processes. These need to be submitted to Professor Deborah Brown (deborah.brown@uq.edu.au) and to the lead tutor, Mikel van Dyken (m.vandyken@uq.edu.au). Draw on megatrends and other data sources to identify the driving forces of your chosen topic of inequality . Identify 2 critical uncertainties , construct a 2 x 2 matrix , and assign quadrants to team members. (4 members per team is the norm but if, due to class numbers, there are 5 team members in a particular group, 2 individuals may work on the same quadrant, but the scenarios produced must then be substantially different from one another.) Teams should meet regularly outside of class time to compare and synthesise results, provide peer feedback to strengthen each quadrant, and begin formulating a group strategy. This is a team assignment as befitting futures thinking and strategic planning in organisational contexts, but teams will be required to delegate tasks to individual members and document individual contributions throughout the scenario planning process. Part B: Scenario Planning Report (Individual scenario + artefact from the future = 2500 words (25%)) Scenario: Students produce individual scenarios, with feedback from peers and mentors. You must demonstrate why each scenario is a plausible future based on current trends, weak or other signals, and imaginative projections. Scenarios must show evidence of integrating philosophical, political, and economic perspectives as well as concepts and principles from the strategic thinking skillset (systems, strategic, entrepreneurial, and futures thinking). Artefact: Choose one kind of artefact from the future (e.g., media release; day-in-the-life vignette; etc) and write a narrative based on the scenario to surface potential and significant secondary consequences. Include this as an inserted text-box in your scenario plan. Individual team members submit their own quadrant + artefact from the future + group strategy to Turnitin while a representative of the group sends a compiled scenario planning report to the lead tutor, Mikel van Dyken (m.vandyken@uq.edu.au). Part C: Groupwork: Group strategy (5%; 500 words) The group strategy should make clear how the strategy could improve equitable outcomes in any of the four scenarios and how it might enable Australia to move toward a preferred future among those captured in the matrix. Part D: Presentation (10%) Student teams will present to the class, including lecturing staff, on the progress of their scenario planning exercise and group strategy in week 10 and receive feedback from the class. Groups have 10 minutes to present. First speaker nominates to introduce the topic and then presents their scenario (~3 minutes), followed by 2 other members of the group (~2 mins). The final speaker presents their scenario and the group strategy (~3 minutes). The order of team presentations will be randomly decided. Other students are tasked with playing Devil's Advocate, stress testing strategies presented to help improve their robustness before submission. Part E: Peer and self evaluation form (300 words; hurdle requirement) Each member of the team will be required to submit a Peer and Self Evalation providing an honest reflection of their contributions and those of their team to the scenario planning process. The evaluation form should reflect the commitments agreed to originally in the Team Charter. Note on AI: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies to assist with research, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will at best provide only limited support and guidance. Students must declare any use of AI on the coversheet to be attached to the front of their individual scenario submission. In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Academic Misconduct: Referencing Fabrication or misrepresentation of sources is considered a breach of academic integrity and may be referred for academic misconduct, regardless of performance in other criteria. This includes but is not limited to: citing non-existent sources, attributing false quotes to real sources, or not including accurate page numbers. Criteria and Marking: Submissions will be assessed according to the following criteria: 1. Ability to construct a well-reasoned and justified scenario. 2. Depth and breadth of knowledge and understanding of central issues. 3. Ability to work collaboratively to produce a well-reasoned strategy to handle all 4 scenarios. 4. Engagement with credible, relevant, and significant academic and other sources of evidence. 5. Insight and/or creativity in constructing a point of view or argument and writing in narrative style. 6. Capacity to produce a coherent and well-written assignment using correct grammar and syntax. 7. Appropriately referenced, as per APA7 (or other standard referencing system) conventions. assessment_details.title: Position paper and policy brief
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific, Work integrated learning. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: It's time to take that strategic, long-term, futures thinking you have been doing and turn it into a concrete plan of action! In the home stretch of the course, students are asked to pull together all that they have learned into two final reports: (a) an individual position paper containing a defensible argument about their problem of inequality and what needs to change and why; and (b) a group-generated policy brief containing an actionable, concrete set of recommendations for a time-poor decision-maker who might be persuaded by (a) but needs to be convinced that it is actionable and plausible before investing more time and resources into it. This is a three-part assignment involving a combination of group and individual work. Part A: Position paper (Individual assignment = 20%; 2500 words) Write a position paper defending your analysis of your chosen problem of inequality and your reasons for advocating changes to policy or practice. A typical structure for a position paper is: thesis statement problem analysis argument(s) for proposed change counterargument(s) defense conclusion Part B: Policy brief (group assignment = 10%; 1500 words) As a group, construct a policy brief to advise a decision-maker of the plausibility of your proposal. A typical structure for a policy brief is: 1 page executive summary Problem statement Options Recommendation(s) Implementation plan/schedule Total word count for both parts (A and B) combined is 4000 words. Week 12 Feedback Event: Teams present overviews of their policy briefs to other teams, mentors, and lecturing staff in week 12 to stress-test their ideas before finalising results and submission. Part C: Complete Peer and Self Evaluation form (hurdle requirement) Update your Peer and Self Evaluation form to capture any adjustments in contributions from team members or yourself and append it to your assignment for submission. assessment_details.ai_statement:
It's time to take that strategic, long-term, futures thinking you have been doing and turn it into a concrete plan of action! In the home stretch of the course, students are asked to pull together all that they have learned into two final reports: (a) an individual position paper containing a defensible argument about their problem of inequality and what needs to change and why; and (b) a group-generated policy brief containing an actionable, concrete set of recommendations for a time-poor decision-maker who might be persuaded by (a) but needs to be convinced that it is actionable and plausible before investing more time and resources into it. This is a three-part assignment involving a combination of group and individual work. Part A: Position paper (Individual assignment = 20%; 2500 words) Write a position paper defending your analysis of your chosen problem of inequality and your reasons for advocating changes to policy or practice. A typical structure for a position paper is: thesis statement problem analysis argument(s) for proposed change counterargument(s) defense conclusion Part B: Policy brief (group assignment = 10%; 1500 words) As a group, construct a policy brief to advise a decision-maker of the plausibility of your proposal. A typical structure for a policy brief is: 1 page executive summary Problem statement Options Recommendation(s) Implementation plan/schedule Total word count for both parts (A and B) combined is 4000 words. Week 12 Feedback Event: Teams present overviews of their policy briefs to other teams, mentors, and lecturing staff in week 12 to stress-test their ideas before finalising results and submission. Part C: Complete Peer and Self Evaluation form (hurdle requirement) Update your Peer and Self Evaluation form to capture any adjustments in contributions from team members or yourself and append it to your assignment for submission. Note on AI: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. Students must declare any use of AI on the coversheet to be attached to the front of their individual scenario submission. In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Academic Misconduct: Referencing Fabrication or misrepresentation of sources is considered a breach of academic integrity and may be referred for academic misconduct, regardless of performance in other criteria. This includes but is not limited to: citing non-existent sources, attributing false quotes to real sources, or not including accurate page numbers. Criteria and Marking: Submissions will be assessed according to the following criteria: 1. Ability to construct a well-reasoned and justified position paper. 2. Depth and breadth of knowledge and understanding of central issues related to the problem. 3. Ability to work collaboratively to produce a credible and actionable policy brief. 4. Engagement with credible, relevant, and significant academic and other sources of evidence. 5. Insight and/or creativity in constructing an original point of view or argument. 6. Capacity to produce coherent and well-written policy documents using correct grammar, syntax, and clear and concise language. 7. Appropriately referenced, as per APA7 (or other standard referencing system) conventions. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Introduction This seminar provides an overview of the course and gives students an opportunity to form into groups of 4, select their design challenge, and create a Team Charter and Peer and Self Evaluation Form. Research design and advanced search techniques will be covered and students will learn about the limits of AI use if working for an Australian government organisation. Students will refamiliarise themselves with argumentation and argument mapping techniques in preparation for the first individual assessment. Learning outcomes: L01

Philosophical perspectives on equality and inequality PROPOSED TOPICS This week explores the question of whether we should think of equality as a value in light of philosophical debates about whether differences in opportunities or outcomes due to luck are justifiable whether it is ever reasonable and ethical to forfeit equality for some other value whether the pursuit of equality is compatible with rights and justifies greater state intrusion into private domains what the true purpose of egalitarian movements is. ACTIVITIES Socratic circle: students discuss philosophical merits of egalitarianism Argument mapping philosophical argument for/against equality as something we should strive toward. Learning outcomes: L01, L05, L06

Political perspectives on equality and inequality PROPOSED TOPICS The many meanings of ‘equality’ in public policy debates Inequality as a value: analyse the diverse ‘problem’ contexts in which ‘equality’ is invoked as a core value, e.g. job incomes, asset ownership, education, health, housing, citizenship rights, Indigenous rights, etc…. Arguments about equality: analyse the political arguments and public perceptions about the interplay/trade-offs between equality and other values ACTIVITIES Consider a range of researchable topics that could inform the future choice of projects on contemporary issues, including ‘Closing the Gap’. Learning outcomes: L01, L05

Economic perspectives on equality and inequality PROPOSED TOPICS Inequality: Trends, Measurement, and Public Perception Redistribution: Trade-offs, Constraints, and Policy Space ACTIVITIES Evidence-based Policy-making: Empirically grounded diagnosis and quantitative thinking. Data in Practice: Students review using data in policy development. Learning outcomes: L01, L05

Systems thinking and mapping Students complete argument mappig assignment in class. PROPOSED TOPICS Systems thinking Systems thinking failures and impacts on decision-making Causal mapping ACTIVITIES Teams create a systems map of their problem of inequality Argument Map to be completed in class (25/08/2026, 12:00).

Strategic thinking PROPOSED TOPICS Strategic thinking, strategic intelligence, and scenario planning Strategic responsiveness, robustness, resilience, and anti-fragility Decision-making under uncertainty Plausibility and future scenarios Causal layered analysis Foresight and strategic intelligence/environment scanning v. forecast Strategic thinking v. strategic planning ACTIVITIES Students conduct a mock scenario planning activity Students commence scenario planning activity for their design challenge

Strategic design thinking PROPOSED TOPICS Entrepreneurial and design thinking Hypothesis formation and falsifiability Prototyping and testing ACTIVITIES Stakeholder engagement planning activity Value proposition canvas exercise/creating a value proposition statement for stakeholders

Values-based policy implementation model PROPOSED TOPICS Integrity systems Political legitimacy and the social license Values-based governance Argumentation as an ethical encounter ACTIVITIES Students conduct an 'ethical audit' of policy documents Learning outcomes: L01, L05, L06

Narrative scenario-building PROPOSED TOPICS The function of narrative techniques (story thinking and telling) in futures thinking--translation rather than invention of matrix; surfacing of secondary consequences Risks of narratives as a futures method -- e.g., false specificity, narrative seduction, dramatic v. mundane outcomes bias, etc. Mitigation strategies ACTIVITIES Students practice translating scenario planning matrix using creative writing techniques Students choose a narrative form appropriate to their scenario to create an artefact from the future (e.g., day-in-the-life vignette; media release; etc) Students pair up to stress test their narratives for too much creative license and to see whether it is apparent what the driving forces and critical uncertainties are (blind inference test).
Team pitch event Teams pitch their individual scenarios and group strategies (15 minutes) with 10 minutes for feedback from other lecturing staff and mentors.

Position papers and policy briefs PROPOSED TOPICS Structure and logic of position papers and policy briefs ACTIVITIES Students practice writing position statements and executive summaries for policy briefs Students stress test their ideas with each other

Position paper and policy brief feedback session ACTIVITIES Teams present their position statements and policy briefs following the sequence of problem, significance, mechanism/action, precedent, timeframe. Lecturers and mentors provide feedback and students refine their positions.
Finalising results ACTIVITIES Students work in teams or individually to prepare final submission. Reflection session on course experience.
